title: A Statistical Approach to Model Selection and Uncertainty Quantification in Neural Networks
text:
This thesis develops a statistical approach to neural-network model selection and interpretation. It brings likelihood-based reasoning, information criteria, hypothesis testing, and uncertainty quantification into the analysis of feedforward neural networks.
The work focuses on selecting parsimonious architectures and inputs, quantifying uncertainty, and making fitted networks easier to interpret through statistically grounded summaries and covariate-effect visualisations.

title: A Statistical Modelling Approach to Feedforward Neural Network Model Selection
text:
Feedforward neural networks (FNNs) can be viewed as non-linear regression models, where covariates enter the model through a combination of weighted summations and non-linear functions. Although these models have some similarities to the models typically used in statistical modelling, the majority of neural network research has been conducted outside of the field of statistics. This has resulted in a lack of statistically-based methodology, and, in particular, there has been little emphasis on model parsimony. Determining the input layer structure is analogous to variable selection, while the structure for the hidden layer relates to model complexity. In practice, neural network model selection is often carried out by comparing models using out-of-sample performance. However, in contrast, the construction of an associated likelihood function opens the door to information-criteria-based variable and architecture selection. A novel model selection method, which performs both input- and hidden-node selection, is proposed using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) for FNNs. The choice of BIC over out-of-sample performance as the model selection objective function leads to an increased probability of recovering the true model, while parsimoniously achieving favourable out-of-sample performance. Simulation studies are used to evaluate and justify the proposed method, and applications on real data are investigated.

title: interpretnn
text:
Description
interpretnn adds statistically grounded inference and interpretation to fitted feedforward neural networks. It provides summary tables, hypothesis tests, confidence intervals, and covariate-effect plots.
The package supports neural networks fitted with nnet, neuralnet, Keras, ANN, and torch.
install.packages("interpretnn")

library(interpretnn)
interpreted_fit <- interpretnn(fit)
summary(interpreted_fit)
plot(interpreted_fit, conf_int = TRUE)

title: Andrew McInerney
section: Neural networks through a statistical lens
text:
Neural networks through a statistical lens
My research sits at the intersection of statistical modelling and machine learning. I develop practical methods that retain the flexibility of neural networks while supporting the questions statisticians care about: which variables matter, how complex should a model be, and how certain are its conclusions?


01

Model selection
Likelihood- and information-criterion-based approaches for selecting inputs and architecture, with an emphasis on parsimony and reproducibility.



02

Statistical inference
Methods for hypothesis testing and uncertainty quantification that make neural-network parameters and predictions more informative.



03

Interpretation
Covariate-effect visualisations and open-source tools that help researchers inspect fitted neural networks as statistical models.

title: selectnn
text:
Description
selectnn implements the model-selection approach developed in McInerney and Burke (2025). The algorithm alternates between selecting hidden-layer complexity and input variables, using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) as its objective.
The package works with feedforward neural networks fitted using nnet and supports both matrix and formula interfaces.
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("andrew-mcinerney/selectnn")

library(selectnn)
fit <- selectnn(y ~ ., data = training_data, Q = 10, n_init = 5)

title: Feedforward Neural Networks as Statistical Models: Improving Interpretability Through Uncertainty Quantification
text:
Feedforward neural networks (FNNs) are typically viewed as pure prediction algorithms, and their strong predictive performance has led to their use in many machine-learning applications. However, their flexibility comes with an interpretability trade-off; thus, FNNs have been historically less popular among statisticians. Nevertheless, classical statistical theory, such as significance testing and uncertainty quantification, is still relevant. Supplementing FNNs with methods of statistical inference, and covariate-effect visualisations, can shift the focus away from black-box prediction and make FNNs more akin to traditional statistical models. This can allow for more inferential analysis, and, hence, make FNNs more accessible within the statistical-modelling context.
